instructions_for_reviewer: SA_Rebuild EN_TRUNC MODERATE — RE-SEGMENT WITH ALIGNED HE+EN PAIRS.
INPUTS (both required)
1) EN_TRUNC_MODERATE_RESEGMENT_KIT.json (or one part; this chunk only)
2) full_dictionary.md (attached by the user — follow it without exception)
DICTIONARY (mandatory — full_dictionary.md)
- Part 1 — abbreviations: expand every Hebrew abbreviation per the dictionary; no raw Hebrew abbreviations in EN.

- Part 2 — halachic terms: use the dictionary transliteration/rendering for every listed term (e.g. muktzeh, melacha, kli rishon, yad soledes bo, psik reisha, d'oraisa, d'rabbanan, l'chatchila, b'dieved).
- Part 3 — commentator names: use names exactly as listed (never anglicize).
- Part 4 — numbers: convert Hebrew letter-numbers to Arabic numerals (siman/seif/daf).
- Part 5 — connectives: render logical connectives per the dictionary.
- Never invent alternate glosses when the dictionary specifies a term.
CONTEXT
- Each case has heSegs > 1 and enSegs === 1 (one EN blob vs multiple HE segments).
- Tier: wave1_moderate — structural split is plausible (high EN/HE ratio) but lacks reliable auto-delimiters; sentence-boundary or semantic alignment required.
- Wave1 strict (24 ids) was already auto-applied or held separately; this kit excludes those.
- Goal: produce heSegs aligned EN segments mapped to each HE slot. Prefer splitting the existing EN blob; translate from HE only where the EN blob clearly lacks material for that HE slot.
TRANSLATION NORMS (when fresh_translate needed)
- Complete: translate every clause; no omissions, summarizing, or paraphrasing away content.
- No additions: no introductions, notes, "Note:", or explanations beyond the source.
- Rama glosses introduced by הגה → {Rama: ...} (curly braces).
- Plain English only — no "Translation:" label, no markdown wrappers around segment text.
- Where norms and full_dictionary.md conflict, full_dictionary.md wins.
TASK
For each case:
1) Align EN to HE slots (index 0 .. heSegs-1).
2) When the existing EN blob clearly contains the translation for a HE slot: split it out (source: split_existing_en). Preserve exact wording where possible.
3) When EN is missing for a HE slot (truncated blob, partial coverage): translate that slot from HE only (source: fresh_translate).
4) When a slot mixes preserved EN cut + gap-fill translation: source: partial.
5) If alignment is unsafe: action needs_human; still return segments[] with best-effort he+en if possible, or empty en for unclear slots.
ACTIONS
- resegment — EN blob splits cleanly into heSegs pieces; no new translation needed.
- mixed_resegment_translate — some slots from EN split, some fresh from HE.
- needs_human — unsafe / ambiguous; flag for manual review.
OUTPUT — JSON array only, same ids/order as input cases:
"action": "resegment" | "mixed_resegment_translate" | "needs_human",
"segments": [
"index": 0,
"source": "split_existing_en" | "fresh_translate" | "partial"
"notes": "short",
"confidence": "high"|"medium"|"low"
CONSTRAINTS
- segments.length MUST equal that case's heSegs (and match he_segments 1:1).
- Each segment object MUST include both he and en side-by-side for evaluation.
- en_segments[] (legacy mirror) should match segments[].en in order when present.
- source on each segment documents whether EN came from blob split vs fresh translation.
- No corpus edits. Return JSON only.

he_segments: ס"ק י"ב יש מגיהים ובתפלת המנחה כ"ע מודים דתמיד קודם לקטורת כדאיתא ביומא. אבל פרשת מנחה י"ל אחר קטורת כצ"ל. ובאמת אם יגיה כן אינו מדוקדק מ"ש דלא כע"ש דהא הע"ש באמת כ"כ לחלוק על דברי הש"ע שכ' תמיד ואח"כ קטורת וע"ז כ' בע"ש ולי נראה שאין הסדר כן אלא תמיד ואח"כ מנח' ואח"כ קטורת ע"ש והכי הו"ל להמג"א למימר ובע"ש כתב די"ל מנחה קודם כו' ואין נראה דהא אביי כו' ולישנא דלא כע"ש משמע שנמשך לדבריו הקודמים שמזה מוכח דלא כע"ש וכן הוא ברוב המקומות במג"א ונלע"ד לפרש דהנה באמת צריך ליתן תבלין בדברי הע"ש דלמה מקדים פרשת מנחה לקטורת ומ"ש בע"ש וע' ברמב"ם הלכות תמידין לא מצאתי דבר ובודאי אין חולק שהקטרת הקטרת היו קודם למנחה והוא ש"ס ערוך. ונראה דהע"ש ס"ל ג"כ דמה שאנו אומרים פרשת תמיד הוא נגד אברים ואף שקטורת קודמין לאברים מ"מ אמרינן פ' תמיד תחלה שהוא מין זבח. וא"כ כיון דבלא"ה אין אנו אומרים כסדר הקרבה בבה"מ ממילא דיש לסמוך פ' מנחה לפרשת התמיד שהמנחה ג"כ היא שייך לקרבן משא"כ הקטורת. ואף שהקטורת קודמים למנחה מ"מ הא בלא"ה אין אנו אומרים כסדר דאל"כ היה צריך לאומרו קודם תמיד ג"כ כאשר הוא באמת הגה' מיי"נ. ולפי מ"ש המג"א דאמירת הפרשה הוא נגד דם התמיד ממילא שהאמירה הוא כסדר ההקרבה וא"כ פשיטא שאין לשנות הסדר וי"ל קטורת קודם מנחה ולכן אחר שהכריע המג"א שהוא כנגד דם התמיד כתב דבמנחה כ"ע מודו שתמיד קודם משום דאיתא ביומא דקטורת של בין הערבים בין אברים לנסכים ועכ"פ האמיר' צריך להיות כסדר ודלא כע"ש שכתב דמנחה קודם לקטורת והיינו משום דס"ל דפ' התמיד נגד האברים והאמירה שלא כסדר דז"א אביי הוה מסדר כו' דם התמיד קודם לקטורת וקטורת לאברים ואברים למנחה. וממ"נ אם הפ' נגד אברים יש להקדים הקטורת קודם לפ' התמיד ג"כ אבל מ"מ אין לומר שלא כסדר א"כ באמת הכפרה בדם ושפיר אמירה שלנו כסדר ודו"ק:

ומה שצ"ע בזה לפע"ד כיון דהמג"א וע"ש מיירי מן המנחה שהיו מקריבין עם תמיד של שחר איזה פ' מנחה יש כאן דפ' מנחת נסכים שבשלח לך אינה ענין למנחת התמיד כלל ע"ש ובמ"ש אא"ז ת"ש ובמנחת התמיד היא אמירה באותו פ' של קרבן התמיד גופו דקאמר ועשירית האיפה סולת למנחה ועיין בש"ס דיומא שם וברש"י שם ופשיטא שאינו עולה על הדעת שיפסיק בפ' קודם ועשירית האיפה ויאמר פ' קטורת באמצע הא ודאי ליתא. וצ"ע:
en_segments: Se'if katan 12. Some emend the text to read: 'Regarding the Minchah prayer, everyone agrees that the tamid precedes the incense, as stated in Yoma; but the passage of the meal offering can be recited after the incense.' In truth, if this is the emendation, the words 'unlike Olat Shabbat' are imprecise. Olat Shabbat itself writes this in disagreement with the Shulchan Aruch, which places the tamid and then the incense. Olat Shabbat writes: 'It appears to me that this is not the order; rather, the tamid is followed by the meal offering and then the incense.' Magen Avraham should therefore have said: 'Olat Shabbat writes that the meal offering should precede, etc., but this does not appear correct, for Abaye, etc.' The phrase 'unlike Olat Shabbat' implies that it follows from Magen Avraham's preceding words that Olat Shabbat is wrong, as is Magen Avraham's usual style. It appears to me as follows. Olat Shabbat's words require explanation: why does he place the passage of the meal offering before the incense? His reference to Rambam's Hilchot Temidin supplies nothing, and no one disputes the explicit Talmudic rule that burning the incense preceded the meal offering. It appears that Olat Shabbat also holds that our recitation of the tamid passage corresponds to the limbs. Although the incense preceded the limbs, we nevertheless recite the tamid passage first because it is a type of sacrifice. Since in any case we do not recite the passages in the Temple's sacrificial order, the meal-offering passage may be placed beside the tamid passage, because the meal offering also belongs to the category of offerings, unlike the incense. Although the incense preceded the meal offering, we are already not following the order; otherwise the incense would also have to be recited before the tamid passage, as Hagahot Maimoniyot indeed states. According to Magen Avraham, however, reciting the tamid passage corresponds to the tamid's blood. The recitation consequently follows the sacrificial order, and it is obvious that the order may not be changed: the incense must precede the meal offering. After Magen Avraham concludes that the passage corresponds to the tamid's blood, he writes that at Minchah everyone agrees the tamid comes first, because Yoma states that the afternoon incense came between the limbs and the libations. In any event, the recitation must follow the order, unlike Olat Shabbat, who places the meal offering before the incense because he holds that the tamid passage corresponds to the limbs and that the recitation does not follow the order. This is incorrect, for Abaye arranged it as follows: the tamid's blood preceded the incense, the incense preceded the limbs, and the limbs preceded the meal offering. Whichever way one turns, if the passage corresponds to the limbs, the incense should also precede the tamid passage; one cannot recite them out of order. The atonement is in fact effected by the blood, so our recitation properly follows the order. Understand this carefully. What remains difficult in my humble opinion is that Magen Avraham and Olat Shabbat discuss the meal offering brought with the morning tamid. What separate meal-offering passage is there? The passage of the libation offering in Parashat Shelach has no relevance to the tamid's meal offering; see there and what my revered grandfather writes in Tevuot Shor. The tamid's meal offering is recited within the tamid passage itself: 'and a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a meal offering.' See the Talmud in Yoma there and Rashi there. It is obviously inconceivable that one should interrupt the passage before 'and a tenth of an ephah' and insert the incense passage in the middle. This certainly cannot be correct and requires further study.

he_segments: ואם יצאו לאחר שהתחיל בקול רם וקדושה יכולין להשלים כל סדר קדושה כו' דהיינו ובא לציון וקדיש שלאחריו:

ותפלת ערבי' לכן אם התחילו והוא רחום בי' ויצאו מקצתן גומרים עד יראו עינינו ואומרים ג"כ קדיש כי הוא שייך לק"ש וברכותיו ותפל' ערבי' בלחש כי אין צריך עשרה לתפל' בלחש אבל אין אומרים קדיש של אחר תפלת י"ח אלא בי' ובעלינו לשבח אף אם פתח בי' ויצאו מקצתן אפ"ה אין אומרי' קדיש יתום שאחריו פחות מעשרה וכן אם אמרו עלינו בלא עשרה א"א אחר כך הקדיש אפילו בי' וכן הדין בתהלים ושיר היחוד אם גמרו אותן בלא י' שאין אומרים קדיש אפי' בי' או איפכא אם היו בתהלים ושיר היחוד י' ובקדיש לא היו י' שאין אומרים והכי נהוג (ל"ח) כמו כן ראיתי נוהגין באיזה מקומות באם אומרים תהלים בלא עשר' שמשייר מזמור א' לאומרו אחר שבאו עשרה והטעם נ"ל דלא אלים קדיש ההוא דהוא מדרבנן לאומרו אף בי' וכן להיפך:
en_segments: If some of the congregation leave after the chazzan has begun the repetition aloud and Kedushah, those who remain may complete the entire order of Kedushah, including U’va LeTzion and the Kaddish that follows it. The same principle applies to Maariv. If they began Vehu Rachum with ten and some then left, they complete the service through Yir’u Eineinu and also recite the Kaddish that follows, because that Kaddish belongs to Shema and its blessings. They may then recite the silent Maariv Shemoneh Esrei, since ten are not required for the silent prayer. The Kaddish following Shemoneh Esrei, however, may be recited only when ten are present. Similarly, even if Aleinu was begun with ten and some then left, the Mourner’s Kaddish that follows may not be recited with fewer than ten. If Aleinu was recited without ten, the Kaddish afterward may not later be recited even after ten arrive. The same applies to Tehillim and Shir HaYichud. If they were completed without ten, the Kaddish afterward may not be recited even if ten are now present. Conversely, if ten were present during Tehillim or Shir HaYichud but were no longer present when the time for Kaddish arrived, the Kaddish is not recited. This is the accepted practice, as stated by Lechem Chamudos. I have likewise seen the practice in some places that when Tehillim is being recited without ten, they leave one chapter of Tehillim to be recited after ten arrive. The reason appears to be that this Kaddish, being of Rabbinic institution, does not possess sufficient force to be recited merely because ten were present earlier, nor does the reverse case permit it.

he_segments: יצא מב"ה וה"ה אם אין שם כהן אלא הוא ג"כ לא ישא את כפיו רק שאינו צריך אז לצאת מב"ה כשאין קוראין כהנים וגם הנוטל ידיהם לא יבא אליו ואז אינו עובר בעשה כמבואר:

ואומרים רבון בשעה שמאריכים בניגון התיבות ויש מי שכתב שלא יאמר כל אחד רבון הנ"ל בשעה שהכהנים עולין לדוכן כי אם דוקא מי שחלם אותו לילה חלום רע אז יאמר רבון כי אף שחלם בשאר ימות השנה אין הביטול מועיל אלא בו ביום כשראה החלום כדאשכחן בתענית חלום דוקא בו ביום או ידלג ב' התיבות חלום חלמתי אלא יאמר רבש"ע אני שלך וחלומותי שלך יר"מ כו' (רא"ש פר' שור שנגח הפרה) וכן נכון בעיני שזה מועיל שאם ראו אחרים חלום רע עליו שמבטלו שאומר בין חלומות שחלמו אחרים עלי כנ"ל כי בלא"ה אין נכון לומר תחנות בשבת וי"ט בחנם כי אסור לעורר עצמו בענייני תחינות השוברות לבו של אדם אבל תפלה ובקשה נופל ג"כ על דברים שמתפלל שיתן לו הקב"ה מתנות רבות יותר מכדי צרכו וזה מותר להתפלל אפילו בשבת וי"ט זה היתה הטעם מסדרי סדר מעמדות שסדרו בשבת בקשות יותר לטוב. כתב לבוש שחיבר מהררמ"י על פירש"י בפ' ואתחנן כתוב בזוהר פרשת נשא כשמתפלל הש"ץ בחזרת תפלת י"ח באם שאין שם נשיאת כפים כשאומר יברכך ה' יראה לצד ההיכל וישמרך לצד ימין שלו. יאר ה' כלפי ההיכל פניו אליך ויחונך יראה לצד שמאלו ליחדו בימין ואסור לשהות כדי הילוך כ"ב אמות בין נטילה לברכה לכן צריך ליטול סמוך לרצה:
en_segments: He should leave the synagogue. The same applies if he is the only kohen present. He should not raise his hands, but in that case he need not leave the synagogue, since no one calls “Kohanim.” The person who washes the kohanim’s hands should likewise not approach him, and he then does not violate the positive commandment, as explained. The prayer beginning “Master of the universe” is recited while the kohanim prolong the words with their melody. Some write that not every person should recite this prayer when the kohanim ascend the platform. Rather, only one who dreamed a bad dream that night should recite it. Even if he dreamed on another night during the year, the annulment is effective only on the very day of the dream, just as a fast for a dream is effective specifically on that day. Alternatively, he should omit the two words “I dreamed a dream,” and say instead: “Master of the universe, I am Yours and my dreams are Yours; may it be Your will,” etc. This is from Rosh, chapter Shor Shenagach Es HaParah. This appears correct to me. It is also effective when others dreamed a bad dream concerning him, because he annuls it by saying, “whether dreams that I dreamed or that others dreamed concerning me.” Otherwise, it is improper to recite gratuitous supplications on Shabbos or Yom Tov, because one may not deliberately arouse himself with matters of supplication that break a person’s heart. Prayer and request, however, also include asking Hashem to grant a person abundant gifts beyond his essential needs, and such requests may be made even on Shabbos and Yom Tov. This is why those who arranged the order of the Maamados included additional requests for good on Shabbos. The Levush, authored by Maharam Yaffe, writes, based on Rashi in parashas Va’eschanan, that the Zohar in parashas Naso states as follows: When the chazzan repeats Shemoneh Esrei and there is no Bircas Kohanim, upon saying “May Hashem bless you,” he should face the aron; upon saying “and protect you,” he should turn toward his right. Upon saying “May Hashem illuminate,” he should face the aron; upon saying “His countenance toward you and favor you,” he should turn toward his left, thereby joining it to the right. It is forbidden to delay between washing and the blessing for the time required to walk twenty two amos. The kohanim must therefore wash close to Retzei.

he_segments: אם הוא חייב היינו באם א"ל הישראל הנה הבית לפניך הניחו במקום שתרצה אבל אם וחד לעכו"ם קרן זוית המיוחד בתוך ביתו להניחו שם אינו זקוק לבער אפילו קיבל הנפקד עליו אחריות דכיון שהשאיל לו מקום מיוחד הוי כאלו אינו ברשותו וכאלו שומר חמצו של עכו"ם בבית עכו"ם וה"מ בחנם אבל בשכר אסור דהא משתכר באיסורי הנאה מכל מקום בדיעבד שקבל שכרו מותר בהנא' (מהרמ"י):

ואפי' חזר והפקידו ביד עכו"ם אחר כו' הגהות אלפסי פ"ק דפסחים. ונ"ל דזהו בודאי פשיטא אם מתחלה נתן העכו"ם חמצו ברשות העכו"ם ושם קיבל עליו ישראל אחריות א"צ לבערו כמ"ש ב"י דאם יחד לו קרן זוית כו' מכל שכן הכא דמתחלה הניח שם חמצו אפי' קיבל עליו ישראל אחריות ויש להביא על זה כמה ראיות ואם אינו חייב באחריות אינו חייב לבערן וצריך לעשות לפניו מחיצה גבוה י' אפי' יחד לו מקום יש להחמיר וצריך מחיצה י' טפחים: כת' מהרי"ץ וזה לשונו במחיל' מכבוד תורתו נ"ל דאין להביא ראיה כלל משם דהתם באשר שהבעלים של חמץ הוא ישראל א"כ גם להיפוך יש מקום קפידא לחול דאם לא יאמר להבעלים הרי שלך לפניך רק הגזלן ישלם לבעליו תמורת החמץ שלו אם כן הבעלים של החמץ יהיה להם הנאה מהחמץ שעבר עליו הפסח דהא יקבל תשלומין מן הגזלן עבור החמץ שלו ולכן אמרי' דאומר לו הרי שלך לפניך זיל שקול חמצך מאי אמרת דהגזלן יקיים מצות ביעור חמץ וכשיהי' מבוער אז יהיה חייב לשלם כמו שהדין הוא בנאבד ולא יהי' חששא דאית לבעלים הנאה בהחמץ בהתשלומין אליו דהא החמץ אינו בעולם. זה אינו רוצה הגזלן לעשות ואמר להיפך להבעלים הרי המצוה לפניך של ביעור חמץ ואתה תקיים המצוה והרי שלך לפניך ואני איני רוצה לשלם לך ממון לשתהיה לך הנאה בממון ומכבדו בהמצות של ביעור חמץ לבעליו של החמץ משא"כ כאן בנידון דידן שאם יחזור ישראל להעכו"ם לא יקוים בו מצות ביעור חמץ ויהא לישראל הנאה במה שיחזיר' להעכו"ם החמץ שלא יהא צריך לשלם ובאמת אין אסור בהנאה ודו"ק:
en_segments: The Jew is liable when he tells the non-Jew, “The house is before you; place it wherever you wish.” If, however, he designates for the non-Jew a specific corner within his house in which to place the chametz, he need not remove it, even if he accepted liability for it. Since he lent the non-Jew a specific place, it is regarded as though the chametz is not in the Jew’s domain, and as though he is guarding a non-Jew’s chametz in the non-Jew’s house. This applies when the place was provided without payment. If the Jew rents the place to him for payment, it is forbidden because he profits from an item from which benefit is prohibited. Nevertheless, after the fact, if he accepted the payment, it is permitted for him to benefit from it. This is from Maharam Yaffe. Even if he later deposited it with another non-Jew, etc. This is from Hagahos Alfasi at the beginning of Pesachim. It appears obvious that if the non-Jew originally placed his chametz in another non-Jew’s domain and the Jew accepted liability for it there, the Jew need not remove it. Beit Yosef writes that if the Jew designated a corner for the non-Jew, he need not remove it, so this case is certainly no more stringent, since the chametz was placed in the non-Jew’s domain from the outset, even though the Jew accepted liability. Many proofs may be brought for this. If the Jew bears no liability, he is not obligated to remove it, but he must place before it a partition ten tefachim high. Even when a specific place was designated for the non-Jew, one should be stringent and require a partition ten tefachim high. Maharitz writes as follows: With due respect to his Torah scholarship, it appears to me that no proof can be brought from that case. There, the owner of the chametz is a Jew. Therefore, there is also a concern in the opposite direction. If the robber does not tell the owner, “Your property is before you,” but instead pays him the value of the chametz, the owner will derive benefit from chametz that remained in existence over Pesach, since he will receive compensation from the robber for it. We therefore say that the robber may tell him, “Your property is before you. Take your chametz.” One might argue that the robber should fulfill the mitzvah of removing chametz, and after destroying it he should become liable to pay, as in a case where the object was lost. There would then be no concern that the owner benefited from the chametz through receiving payment, since the chametz would no longer exist. The answer is that the robber does not wish to do so. Instead, he tells the owner: “The mitzvah of removing the chametz is before you. You fulfill the mitzvah, and your property is before you. I do not wish to pay you money and thereby cause you to benefit through money.” He therefore honors the owner of the chametz with the mitzvah of removing it. That case is unlike ours. Here, if the Jew returns the chametz to the non-Jew, the mitzvah of removing chametz will not be fulfilled. The Jew will benefit by returning the chametz because he will thereby avoid liability to pay. In truth, however, such benefit is not prohibited. Consider this carefully.

en_segments: This too is stated there. He writes that we do not say that because, according to the claimant, he is wicked, he cannot be believed under oath. The same is written in Choshen Mishpat, siman 82, seif 10. In my humble opinion, this does not disagree with what was written above at the end of siman 169. There, he claims that he took the money permissibly and specifies the basis of permission, namely that he took it through a non-Jew, and he is believed by analogy to the law of a prozbul. Here, however, and in siman 82, he denies everything and does not claim that he took it permissibly, so an oath is administered. As for Rama's words, "and some disagree," I did not merit to see his source in Darkei Moshe.

he_segments: אם נותן כו'. שם ס"ח ב' ועתוס' שם ד"ה מקום. ור"ח גרים כו' פי' אם היו כו'. ולכאורה משמע דלתועלת הנותן קאמר דהוא בכלל הקרן לנותן וכן פי' בתוספת הרא"ש אבל הטור פי' דלתועלת המקבל קאמר שאם היו פירות של המקבל מונחים ברשותו והנותן נותן לו מעות בשבילן צריך לשום כפי מה שהיה צריך ליתן בשוק עם שכר כתף וכ' וכ"ש אם יש למקבל כו' כמ"ש בסכ"ב. והרמב"ם פי' בדרך אחר ע"ש:

(ליקוט) אם כו'. גירסת ר"ח ורי"ף וש"פ בברייתא מקום שנהגו להעלות שכר כתף למעות מעלין לבהמה מעלין להעלות ולדות בשכר עמלו ומזונו מעלין. ועתוס' שם בשם ר"ח ומפרש הטור לטובת המקבל כמו בסיפא. ב"י. וכתב הטור אם נותן כו' כמ"ש כאן וכ' ואפילו היתה העיסקא בבית המקבל מעלה אותן כשער שבשוק כו' והן שני פירושים פי' הראשון שכ' הטור וכאן בש"ע הוא כפי' הרמב"ם וכמ"ש בב"ח דברי הרמב"ם שבכל פעם שמוליך המקבל בשוק למכור העיסקא אם דרך לשכור כו' צריך ליתן כו'. ופי' השני הוא פי' ר"ח לדברי הטור והוא להוליך משוק הסחורה כשלוקח ומוליך לביתו ורישא הוא כשמוליך לשוק ואע"ג שבתוס' כ' מבית הנותן והטור כתב מן השוק הכל ענין אחד וב"ח ודו"פ פי' בע"א ול"נ (ע"כ):
en_segments: If he gives, etc. There 68b; and Tosafot there s.v. place. And Rashi HaChadash, etc., explained: if they were, etc. And at first glance it implies for the giver's benefit he speaks, that it is included in the principal for the giver; and likewise explained in Tosafot of the Rosh. But Tur explained for the recipient's benefit he speaks, that if the recipient's produce were placed in his possession and the giver gives him money on their account he must assess according to what he would need to give in the market with porter wages; and he wrote: and all the more so if the recipient has, etc., as written in seif 22. And the Rambam explained in another manner, see there. (Likkut) If, etc. Rashi HaChadash's and Rif's and Shulchan Arukh's version in the baraita: a place where they practiced to raise porter wages for money, they raise for an animal, they raise to raise offspring with his labor wages and his food they raise. And Tosafot there in name of Rashi HaChadash; and Tur explains for the recipient's benefit as in the latter clause. Beit Yosef. And Tur wrote "if he gives," etc., as written here; and he wrote: and even if the iska were in the recipient's house he raises them at the market rate, etc.; and these are two explanations, the first explanation that Tur wrote; and here in Shulchan Arukh it is like the Rambam's explanation; and as Beit Chadash wrote the Rambam's words that whenever the recipient carries to the market to sell the iska, if it is customary to hire, etc., he must give, etc. And the second explanation is Rashi HaChadash's explanation of Tur's words, to carry from the merchandise market when he takes and carries to his house; and the first clause is when he carries to the market; and even though in Tosafot it is written from the giver's house and Tur wrote from the market, all one matter; and Beit Chadash and D.M. explained with one explanation; and in my humble opinion (end).

he_segments: אם התנו כו'. רמב"ם וכמש"ש אי פלגא באגר כו' אי כו' ונמצא שלעולם נוטל שתות השכר כולו יותר על חלקו שהוא בתורת מלוה וכן בהפסד פורע הנותן שתות יותר שהוא שליש חלק של א' מהן וכ' רבותיו של הרמב"ם שאותו שליש מחשבין מחלק הנותן שהוא פקדון והוא שליש חלקו בין בשכר בין בהפסד ולכן בכה"ג שכ' כאן בש"ע שהתנו שיטול המתעסק רביע נמצא שחלק של פקדון הוא שלשה חלקים בהפסד משלם הנותן כולו. ורמב"ן ורשב"א ס"ל בהיפך דהשליש הנ"ל מחשבין מחלק המלוה בין בשכר בין בהפסד לפיכך משלם בכה"ג המתעסק שתות אלא בסיפא שהתנו בהפסד רביע נוטל בריוח שליש שהוא חלקו ושליש חלקו אבל הרמב"ם הקשה על רבותיו שא"כ פעמים שישלם הנותן יותר על ההפסד כגון אם התנה שיטול א' משבע בריוח ויהיה הפסד שבעה דינרין וישלם הנותן שמנה דינרין וכיוצא וכן קשה כה"ג על הרמב"ן ורשב"א שפעמים יטול המתעסק יותר מהריוח כגון שהתנו שיפסיד הנותן א' משבעה והרויחו שבעה דינרין צריך שיטול המתעסק שמנה דינרין ע"כ פי' הרמב"ם שאם התנו על הריוח בהפסד יוסיף הנותן שליש מחלק חבירו שהוא מלוה ואם התנו על ההפסד יטול המתעסק שליש מחלק חבירו שהוא פקדון וז"ש יפסיד כו' יטול כו' וכן הוא הסברא בהרוחה נוטל התוספת מחלק חבירו וכן בהפסד מפסיד הנותן היתרון בחלק חבירו לכן משערינן הכל בחלק חבירו אבל הרמב"ן והרשב"א תי' קושית הרמב"ם דלעולם אין משלם הנותן יותר מההפסד או הריוח וכה"ג כ' בח"מ סי' קע"ו ס"ו וע"ש בסי' צ"ג סי"ג דרמב"ם פליג שם וס"ל דישלם מביתו:

(ליקוט) אם התנו כו'. ושיטה אחרת לסמ"ג עב"י וכ' בכ"מ וטעמו של הרמב"ם דבריוח יטול שליש מחלק הפקדון יותר דהא אותו העודף נוטל בשכר טרחו בחלק הפקדון לכן נוטל מחלק הפקדון בין רב בין מעט לפי החלק של הפקדון משא"כ בהפסד שאינו נוטל כלום בריוח אלא שבשכר טרחו מנכה לו מהפסד שלו שלא יפסיד כ"כ מנכה לו לפי ההפסד של המקבל בחלקו כ"כ מנכה לו שליש בהפסדו שלעולם לא יפסיד אלא ב' שלישים מחלקו של המקבל. ועבב"י שי"מ ההיא דפלגא באגר ותילתא כו' דל"ד שיהא לו שתות יתר בשכר מבהפסד אלא דבר מועט וע"ש בדבריו שפי' דברי הרי"ף והרא"ש כדברי הרמב"ם והטור ודבריו אינן נראין (ע"כ):
en_segments: If they stipulated, etc. Rambam; and as written "if half in profit," etc., "if," etc.; and it results that always he takes a sixth of all the wages more than his share which is as a loan; and likewise in loss the giver pays a sixth more which is a third of one of their shares. And the Rambam's teachers wrote that that third is calculated from the giver's share which is the deposit, and it is a third of his share both in wages and in loss; therefore in such a case where it is written here in Shulchan Arukh that they stipulated the dealer shall take a quarter, it results that the deposit share is three parts in loss, the giver pays all. And Ramban and Rashba hold the opposite: that the said third is calculated from the lender's share both in wages and in loss; therefore in such a case the dealer pays a sixth. But in the latter clause where they stipulated a quarter in loss he takes a third in profit which is his share and a third of his share. But the Rambam challenged his teachers that otherwise sometimes the giver will pay more than the loss, for example if they stipulated he take one of seven in profit and the loss is seven dinars, the giver will pay eight dinars and similar; and likewise he challenges Ramban and Rashba that sometimes the dealer will take more than the profit, for example they stipulated the giver lose one of seven and they profited seven dinars, the dealer must take eight dinars; therefore the Rambam explained that if they stipulated on profit, in loss the giver adds a third from his fellow's share which is a loan; and if they stipulated on loss, the dealer takes a third from his fellow's share which is the deposit; and this is what is written "he shall lose," etc., "he shall take," etc.; and likewise is the reasoning: in profit he takes the addition from his fellow's share; and likewise in loss the giver loses the surplus in his fellow's share, therefore we estimate everything according to his fellow's share. But Ramban and Rashba answer the Rambam's difficulty that never does the giver pay more than the loss or the profit; and likewise Choshen Mishpat siman 176 seif 6; and see there siman 93 seif 13 that the Rambam disagrees there and holds he pays from his own house. (Likkut) If they stipulated, etc. And another method for Semag, and Kesef Mishneh wrote the Rambam's reason: in profit he takes a third more from the deposit share, for that surplus he takes as labor wages on the deposit share; therefore he takes from the deposit share whether much or little according to the deposit share's portion, not so in loss where he takes nothing in profit except that from his labor wages he deducts from his loss so he does not lose so much, he deducts according to the recipient's loss in his share; so much he deducts a third in his loss so he never loses except two-thirds of the recipient's share. And on Beit Yosef siman 176 that incident of half in profit and a third, etc., he does not hold that he should have a sixth extra in wages than in loss but something small; and see there in his words that he explained the Rif's and Rosh's words like the Rambam's and Tur's words, and his words do not appear correct (end).

(°) פי' אם לא נתרצית קודם פסח ונתרצית אחר הפסח אינו מחויב לקדשה כיון שעבר הזמן וכמ"ש לעיל בסי' רכ"ח סעיף מ"א שאם לא הי' מחוייב בדבר בלא שבועה זו ועבר היום שוב אין חיוב שבועה עליו ומיגו דחיילא אאחר הפסח חיילא נמי אקודם הפסח באיסור כולל וכשהשבועה היא לתועלת האשה או ע"י שידוכין שבלי ספק היה לתועלתה וכדי שלא תתבייש אזי צריך התרה אפילו עבר הזמן כדעת הי"א שם וכמ"ש שם בשם הריב"ש לדעת הרא"ש כנלע"ד:
en_segments: The statement of Rava there, Shevuot 24b. If she did not consent before Pesach but consented afterward, he is not obligated to betroth her, because the designated time has passed. As explained above in siman 228, seif 41, when he had no independent obligation apart from the oath and the day passed, the oath no longer obligates him. en_segments: Or she married before beit din and they did not object. This wording implies that if she married privately without beit din's knowledge and afterward witnesses came that she had been taken captive, she must leave the marriage. Just as a married woman against whom witnesses of captivity later appear must leave, so too a captive woman who married must leave unless she married by authorization of beit din or in their presence without objection. In truth, however, there is room to distinguish. A married woman is not believed because she is personally interested in remaining with her husband. A captive woman who has already married does not abandon a permitted option and deliberately choose a prohibited one, for she was free to marry any Israelite she wished. Responsa Radach, house 8, writes that even if she married privately without beit din's knowledge she need not leave. The Radach also writes that even if her husband knew before marriage that she had been captive, so long as the fact was not established before beit din by witnesses she remains permitted to him, because she had a migo that she could have married another man. It appears, however, that if a married woman was taken captive and her husband knew that fact, she is not believed to say she remained pure, because she has no migo to say she was never captive. This is also implied by Responsa Rosh, rule 32, siman 5: once the husband knows that she was among the gentiles, there can be no greater testimony of captivity than that.

See there also regarding the Shach’s conclusion that a kinyan cannot create an obligation to swear, and what I wrote concerning the words of Machaneh Ephraim. The Mechaber’s statement here that some authorities impose liability for negligence is based on the view that one who is negligent is treated as one who directly causes damage. In my addenda to Even HaEzer I proved from Avodah Zarah 71b that negligence can indeed be treated as damaging. There, seif 40: some authorities impose liability for negligence. This is the Rambam’s view. In Hilchot Maaseh HaKorbanot 14:5 he writes that one who vows a korban and designates it remains responsible if it is lost or stolen until it is offered, whereas one who merely dedicates a voluntary offering is not responsible if it dies or is stolen. It is noteworthy that with the voluntary offering the Rambam writes “dies or is stolen,” rather than stating the stronger case that even if he was negligent he is exempt. This suggests that the Rambam regards him at least as a shomer chinam, liable for negligence, consistent with the Rambam’s broader position that negligent custodianship is a form of damaging. Although one who damages consecrated property is exempt from the laws of meilah and the added fifth, he can remain liable for the principal loss. The later case of one who says, “I undertake to offer it in the temple of Chonyo,” and nevertheless fulfills his vow, is different because by expressly stipulating that condition he is treated as having stipulated that he will not bear ordinary responsibility even if he causes the loss through the specified act. Without such an express condition, one who says “this animal is an offering” can still be liable if he damages it directly or is negligent. There is also room to examine whether one who says, “I undertake to bring an olah,” remains liable if the designated animal dies through a complete accident. The Rambam’s initial phrase mentions loss or theft and does not mention death, which could imply exemption for a true accident. Yet in the second clause he says that a voluntary offering is exempt if it dies or is stolen, implying by contrast that a vowed offering remains liable even if it dies. One can reconcile the wording by saying that in the first clause the Rambam wished to teach that the vower must replace the animal immediately even when it was merely lost or stolen and might later be found. He cannot postpone until after the festival on the hope that it will reappear, because his personal responsibility remains and he may violate bal te’acher. In the second clause the Rambam adds the case of death to teach that even where the animal certainly will never return, the voluntary donor has no further liability. His choice of theft there hints that the death contemplated is not necessarily a total accident, and perhaps a genuinely unavoidable death would exempt even the one who said “harei alai.” The Rambam also deliberately departs from the Mishna’s wording, which uses death in both clauses. This requires further study. There, in the same seif: if they made a kinyan that he would be obligated like custodians. The Shach writes that a kinyan to impose an oath is ineffective because it is merely a kinyan on words. Machaneh Ephraim cites Mahara’sh and the Shach and asks from siman 22, where a kinyan to swear is treated as binding. The matters must be distinguished. At first one might answer, as Urim VeTumim and Netivot do, that an undertaking to swear is ultimately monetary because if he refuses the oath he must pay, so the kinyan is on money rather than mere words. Yet the deeper point is that in our case the monetary liability is itself an asmachta. A kinyan works because, in return for the trust placed in him, the custodian genuinely undertakes responsibility. That reasoning is sufficient where there is only one uncertainty, whether the item will be stolen. But if the undertaking is framed as “I will swear if it is stolen,” and one seeks to derive a monetary obligation from failure to swear, there are two contingencies: perhaps it will never be stolen, and even if it is, perhaps he will swear. The benefit of being trusted is not enough to overcome such a double asmachta. Thus the kinyan cannot be sustained as a monetary undertaking, while as an undertaking merely to perform an oath it is a kinyan on words. Siman 22 is different because the claim already exists when the kinyan is made. There is no future contingency and no asmachta of this sort. Therefore a kinyan to swear there can be effective because refusal to swear immediately entails payment. This also explains why the Shach’s discussion in siman 291 does not contradict his words here. There the kinyan was to assume monetary liability as a paid custodian, which can take effect. The remaining question is only whether, by voluntarily accepting that monetary status, he also accepted the ordinary oath that accompanies it. Perhaps he intended liability only upon admission and not liability based upon an evidentiary presumption. That is a separate issue from whether a direct kinyan on a future oath can take effect. Examine this carefully.

The Maggid Mishneh writes that no Torah oath applies because the debtor granted credibility, and that only a heset oath applies whether he denies everything or admits part. Many have wondered why this credibility should be stronger than an oral claim. Its effect is only to neutralize the document; it should not exempt a partial admitter from the Torah oath. The Bach answers that the Torah oath for partial admission rests on the presumption that a person does not brazenly deny his creditor. Here, because the creditor trusted him, he is willing to deny; therefore even on a partial admission he is believed with a heset oath through the migo that he could have denied all. This is difficult, for by that reasoning even a heset oath should not be required, as the Gemara says concerning a claim against one’s son: since a person is bold toward the son, a partial admitter is like one returning a lost object and is exempt even from heset. The glossator answers that the cases are not comparable. A finder is exempt for public policy, and a defendant against the son is exempt from the newly generated partial-admission oath, whether because of the lack of brazenness or because of a migo. But no one suggested that his partial admission should exempt him from the oath he would have owed had he denied everything. In my opinion, the ordinary credibility granted to the debtor includes both a claim that he paid all and a claim that he paid part, as explained in siman 84, seif 5. Just as one claiming full payment swears only heset, so too one claiming partial payment, for the clause treats both alike. Although the Tur says the matter becomes like an oral claim, he means only that the credibility clause does not exempt the debtor from an oath altogether. The glossator offers another sound reason. If the debtor were required to take a Torah oath, he could not reverse it onto the creditor. If he declined to swear, he would have to pay without any oath by the creditor. The credibility clause would thus worsen his position, because without it the creditor could not collect without swearing. It is untenable to make the debtor choose between a Torah oath and requiring the creditor to swear, since the two consequences are inseparable.

סעיף א הקובע זמן לחברו וכו'. נ"ב ע' בש"ך סק"א מה שמשיג על הסמ"ע ולפענ"ד דבריו תמוהין דודאי צדקו דברי הסמ"ע דבטוען המלוה שמא נאמן הלוה אף בתוך זמנו. כיון דחזקת ממון מסייע לו אמרינן ברי ושמא ברי עדיף. דבהדי חזקה אמרי' ברי עדיף וכמ"ש הש"ס בפ"ק דכתובות גבי משארסתני נאנסתי דהיכי דאיכא חזקה דגופא בהדי ברי ושמא ברי עדיף אף דמצד עצמו הוי חזקה דממונא עדיף מחזקה דגופא מ"מ בהצטרף בהדי ברי מהני ה"ה נמי הכא. אף דת"ז עדיף מחזקה דממונא מ"מ בהצטרף בהדי ברי ושמא עדיף. ומה שמביא הש"ך ראיה מיורשים דבריו תמוהין ובמחכת"ה נעלם ממנו סוגית הש"ס והרא"ש וכל הקדמונים דרפ"ב דכתובות דקאמר שם הש"ס לימא מתני' דלא כר"ג וכו'. ומשני אפי' תימא ר"ג וכו'. ע"כ לא קאמר ר"ג אלא בברי ושמא אבל הכא ברי וברי היא. והקשו הכל דתינח נתגרשה אבל נתארמלה הרי טוענין היורשין שמא יתרצו כיון דאנן טענינן ליורשים כל מה דמצי אביהן למיטען חשוב כטענת ברי. וכ"כ שם הרא"ש להדיא ובשיטה מקובצת בשם כל הקדמונים א"כ מוכרח דהיכי אמרינן ברי ושמא ברי עדיף מ"מ טענות היורשים חשיב כטענת ברי ולכך גבי יורשים ודאי שייך הך חזקה דאין אדם פורע ת"ז ולא כשהוא בעצמו היה טוען שמא וצדקו דברי הסמ"ע. מיהו בחידושי משפט צדק לחו"מ סימן נ"ט שם העלתי דהיכי דהוא חוב בשטר ותו"ז כיון דאיכא חזקות. חזקה דשטרי בידך מה בעי וחזקה דתו"ז אז הדר ה"ל חזקת ממון חדא במקום תרתי ולאו כלום הוא ושוב לא אמרי' ברי עדיף ובזה גובה המלוה אף כשטוען שמא. וז"ב ונכון לדינא: שם ס"א והניח יתומים אפי' קטנים. נ"ב עבש"ך סק"ב מה שנסתפק בשם המוהרשד"ם באם הגיע הזמן ונתחסד המלוה עם הלוה להאריך לו הזמן אם שייך בהזמן הב' אין אדם פורע תוך זמנו. והקצה"ח פשט ליה מדברי הנ"י שכ' בקבע זמן בשעת הלואה אז אח"כ עש"ה. והנה לדעתי אין זה כלום. דהנ"י כוונתו כגון דתחלה לא קבעו זמן כלל רק הלוה לו סתם ולא שאלו על איזה זמן ואחר כך פגעו זה בזה וקבעו זמן אז בזה נחשב זה כקביעת זמן בשעת הלואה והוי כהוכיח סופו על תחלתו כאלו קבעו בשעת ההלואה כיון שלא היה קביעת זמן אחר תחלה דדרך כל הלואה לקבוע זמן ואם כן מה שקבעו אחר כך הוי כאילו קבעו תחלה וכ"ש אם דברו בשעת הלואה שמלוה לו ע"ת מה שיקבעו אחר כך זמן כשיהיה להם פנאי וזה הוי כקביעת זמן בשעת ההלואה. אבל אם מתחלה בשעת הלואה קבעו זמן ואח"כ קבעו זמן שני בזה נ"ל שפיר כדעת המוהרשד"ם. אך מן הש"ס יש להביא ראיה דמאי פריך שם אילימא בזמנו פשיטא אלא לאו תוך זמנו וכו'. ודילמא מיירי שקבעו זמן שני וקמ"ל דאף שהוא תו"ז שני נאמן לומר פרעתי ובע"כ מוכח דאין חילוק בין זמן ראשון לזמן שני. ודוק היטב: שם סעיף א' בהג"ה אבל אם היה מעות מופקדין בידו ועוסק בהם לצורך אחרים האי כשאר פקדון וכו' נ"ב עיין כאן בש"ך סק"י מה שהשיג על המהר"א ששון בדין סחור' אם שייך בי' אין אדם פורע ת"ז ועיין בחיבורי לחו"מ מהדורא ה' סימן קע"ט מ"ש להחזיק דברי המהר"א ששון ועכ"פ המוחזק יכול לומר קים לי' ע"ש ודוק:
en_segments: Seif 1: One who fixes a time for his fellow and demands payment within the time. Note: See my second-edition work on Choshen Mishpat, at the end, siman 182, where I proved that according to Rashi, although as practical halacha we rule that a migo is accepted even against a presumption, nevertheless a Torah-level oath is required. See there for the reasoning. Seif 1: One who fixes a time for his fellow, etc. See Shach, seif katan 1, who challenges the Sema. In my humble opinion his words are difficult. The Sema is certainly correct that where the lender himself is uncertain, the borrower is believed even if he claims to have paid within the fixed time. Since the presumption of possession supports the borrower, the combination of a definite claim and an uncertain claim favors the definite claim. We find similarly in the first chapter of Ketubot concerning the claim “I was violated after betrothal”: where a bodily presumption supports the definite claimant against the other party’s uncertain claim, the definite claim prevails. Although a presumption of monetary possession is ordinarily stronger than a bodily presumption, when the latter is joined to a definite claim it can prevail. The same applies here. Although the presumption that a person does not pay within the time is stronger than ordinary monetary possession, when monetary possession is joined to a definite claim against an uncertain claim, it prevails. The Shach’s proof from heirs is also difficult. With respect, he overlooked the Gemara, the Rosh, and the early authorities at the beginning of the second chapter of Ketubot. The Gemara asks whether the Mishna is not in accordance with Rabban Gamliel and answers that even Rabban Gamliel may agree, because he rules only where one side is definite and the other uncertain, whereas here it is definite against definite. The commentators ask that this explains a divorced woman, but if she was widowed the heirs are uncertain. They answer that since we plead on behalf of heirs whatever their father could have pleaded, their plea is regarded as a definite plea. The Rosh says this expressly, and the Shita Mekubetzet cites all the early authorities accordingly. Thus, even where a definite claim would normally prevail against uncertainty, the heirs’ pleading is considered definite. Consequently, with heirs the presumption that a person does not pay within the time certainly applies, whereas it need not apply where the debtor himself admits uncertainty. The Sema is therefore correct. However, in my Chiddushei Mishpat Tzedek on Choshen Mishpat, siman 59, I concluded that where the debt is evidenced by a document and the claim is payment within the time, two presumptions support the lender: the presumption expressed by “why is your document in my hand?” and the presumption that a person does not ordinarily pay before the due date. The debtor’s monetary possession is then only one presumption against two and has no force. In such a case we no longer say that the definite claim prevails, and the lender collects even where he is uncertain. This is clear and correct as practical halacha. There, seif 1: and he left heirs, even minors. See Shach, seif katan 2, who cites Maharshal’s doubt where the original due date arrived and the lender graciously extended the term, whether during the second term we still apply the presumption that a person does not pay before the due date. Ketzot HaChoshen resolves the issue from the Nimukei Yosef, who speaks of a time fixed at the time of the loan. In my opinion that proof is not decisive. The Nimukei Yosef can mean a case where originally no time was fixed at all. The lender made an ordinary loan without discussing a term, and only later when they met they fixed a due date. Since there had been no earlier term, and loans ordinarily contemplate a time for payment, the later fixing of the time reveals the original arrangement and is considered as though the term had been fixed at the loan’s inception. All the more so if at the time of the loan they expressly agreed that the loan would run until a time they would later fix when convenient. That too is effectively a term fixed at the loan’s inception. But where they originally fixed one due date and later agreed on a second due date, it seems to me that Maharshal’s doubt remains. Nevertheless, a proof may be brought from the Gemara. It asks, “If the case is at the due date, that is obvious; rather, is it not within the due date?” Why not answer that the case concerns a second fixed period, teaching that even within the second period the borrower is believed to say he already paid? It follows that there is no distinction between the first and second fixed terms. Examine this carefully. There, seif 1 in the gloss: but if money was deposited with him and he uses it for the needs of others, it is like any other deposit, etc. See Shach, seif katan 10, who challenges Maharam Alshakar regarding merchandise and whether the presumption that a person does not pay within the fixed time applies to it. See my fifth-edition work on Choshen Mishpat, siman 179, where I defended Maharam Alshakar. In any event, the party in possession can say that he relies upon that view.

שוב ראיתי בא"ע סימן צ"ו סט"ו מביא הר"ב גופיה דעת ה' המגיד פ' ט"ז מה' אישות דס"ל דבדבר שא"י לכפור לא הוי מ"מ אפי' ליכא שעבוד קרקעות ואזיל לטעמי' בפ"ד מה' טוען ומביאו ב"י שם ע"ש וכן משמע בתשו' מבי"ט ח"ב ס"ס ר"ה ואם כן נרא' פשוט לענין דינא דאין לחייבו ש"ד דלא יהא אלא ספיקא דדינא הוי קולא לנתבע:
en_segments: Even if it contains a clause of credibility, etc. In my humble opinion this ruling requires study. It appears that the Mechaber ruled this way based on what he wrote in Bedek HaBayis, that perhaps the Rambam also agrees. In truth, however, it appears to me that the Rambam holds that a handwritten obligation containing a credibility clause is heilech, because the Rambam explains the reason as being that the defendant cannot deny it. The Maggid Mishneh and Nimukei Yosef at the beginning of Bava Metzia also explain the Rambam this way, contrary to Bedek HaBayis's understanding. Lechem Mishneh, chapter 4 of Hilchos To'en, likewise understands the Rambam this way. His challenge there to the Nimukei Yosef, as though the Nimukei Yosef did not understand the Rambam that way, is puzzling, for the Nimukei Yosef actually writes exactly this. I later saw that the Kesef Mishneh in chapter 22 of Hilchos Edus likewise understands the Rambam as I have written, and I cited his words above in siman 31, seif 2. Rabbeinu Yeruham also reaches this conclusion in Nesiv 3, chelek 2, writing that some authorities hold that whenever one admits something he could not have denied, such as a handwritten obligation with a credibility clause, it is heilech and he is exempt from a Torah oath, and that the Rambam writes so. Rabbeinu Yeruham later states this ruling without qualification at the end of that section. The Rosh at the beginning of the second chapter of Kesubos likewise holds that something which the defendant cannot deny is heilech, as cited by the Beit Yosef above at the beginning of siman 87. The Maggid Mishneh in chapter 5 of Hilchos To'en holds the same, contrary to the marginal note here in the Sema that cites him for the opposite. See there. The gloss in siman 87, seif 1, likewise appears to rule this way, following the Tur. The Semag explicitly writes that a document is heilech because denial cannot avail against it, without mentioning any land lien. Maadanei Yom Tov at the beginning of Bava Metzia likewise writes that according to the Rosh and Rambam, whenever the defendant cannot deny the admitted portion it is not considered a partial admission, even without a formal document. The Bach also writes that this is the view of the Rambam, Rosh, and Tur. I later saw that in Even HaEzer, siman 96, seif 15, the Rama himself cites the Maggid Mishneh in chapter 16 of Hilchos Ishus as holding that where the defendant cannot deny a matter, it is not a partial admission even when there is no land lien, consistent with the Maggid Mishneh's approach in chapter 4 of Hilchos To'en, as cited by the Beit Yosef there. The responsa of Mabit, volume 2, end of siman 205, likewise appear to support this. Accordingly, the practical ruling is plainly that he cannot be obligated in a Torah oath. At the very least it is a matter of legal doubt, and in a doubt concerning an oath we rule leniently for the defendant.

This oath for a hired worker was instituted by the Sages for the worker's livelihood, and also because an employer is occupied with his affairs and workers and can easily forget whether he paid. The Sages applied the rule uniformly even to an employer who is not especially preoccupied, and even where the employer denies everything. If the employer has one supporting witness, see Tumim, seif katan 16, where it appears that the worker does not swear and collect. The matter requires study.

he_segments: שאלה מן הרב מהר"ר יששכר אב"ד דק"ק ארלא לא"א מ"ו הרב המחבר ז"ל וזה נוסחו . שלם לאהובי אדוני הגאון מהר"ר משה ש"ן בהיותי פה אירע כמה פעמים לסדר גט ומנעתי עצמי מלכתוב פה עבור קריאת שם המקום שחקרתי ודרשתי בכל שטרי כתובות וק"ס שנכתבי' מקדמוני' פה נכתב כל ארלא באל"ף תחלה וסוף ולפי ספרי הערכ"י של כותים חקרתי ודרשתי שהוא נכתב ארלע בע' בסוף א"כ איזה מהם לבד שנכתוב יש לחוש לשינוי שם עירו שהוא פסול גמור ובודאי שאין לדמות זה לרעד"ש והרעד"ש (הנזכר פה בסעיף ג') שהתם לא נשתנה קריאת שם העיר בנקודה בין שם ישראל לבין שם של כותים רק כותים קורין הרעדש בה' וישראל קורין רעדיש בלא ה' וזה אינו אלא קיצור לשון משא"כ בנ"ד שנשתנה בקריאת הנקודה כי א' בסוף אז הל' שלפניו נקרא בקמ"ץ ואם ע' בסוף הקריא' של ל' היא כמו בסגול ולכן נראה דעתי שיש לכתוב ארלא דמתקרו ארלע ולא רציתי לסמוך למעשה על דעתי לבד יודיעני רום מכ"ת דעתו בזה וגם יש כאן מים ואין לו שום שם אבל נראה שאין לחוש לזה בשביל שאינו רק מים הנקר' טיי"ך בל"א והוא בכלל מי מעינות כמו שהוא בתשובת מהרי"ק וא"כ יש לכתוב כאן מי בארות ומי מעינו' ולא שום שם נהר ולכן באתי לבקש שיודיענו רום מכ"ת דעתו הרמה בכל זה ע"כ השאלה:

תשובה ראיתי דברי מעלתך אשר נסתפק אם לכתוב בגט ארלא או ארלע הנה יעיין מעלתך בתשובת הר' מהרי"ק ובפסקי מהרא"י (אשר מהם נובעים דברי הרב בהג"ה כאן) יראה להדיא ששם הקבוע לה בלשון העברי הוא העיקר והנה רוטנבורק הנקרא בלשון עברי בסוף בק' ובל' הכותי' לבסוף בג' יש הפרש ביניהם באות א' וכן טויברא וטוברא הנזכר שם בפסקי מהרא"י יש הפרש ביניהם בשינוי נקודו' כמבואר שם וכן קאזמר דמתקרי קאזימרו בנוסח גט קראקא יש הפרש כמה אותיות אבל הפרש נקודה אחת ודאי אזלינן בתר ל' עברי ע"כ מצאתי ובודאי עוד היה להרב א"א מ"ו המחבר מילין בדבר זה ונטרפ' השנה וה' ירוה צמאונינו והעתקתי דבריו המעטים להלכה ולא למעשה:
en_segments: A responsum from the eminent Rabbi Yissachar, av beit din of the holy community of Arla, to my father and teacher, the author. The question was: In Arla, when arranging a get, I refrained several times because of uncertainty about spelling the city's name. In old ketubot and other Jewish documents written here, the name is always written "Arla," with alef at the beginning and end. In the gentile registers, however, I investigated and found it written "Arle," with ayin at the end. If we write only one form, perhaps we change the city's name, which is a complete invalidation. This cannot be compared to the example of Radash and HaRadash mentioned here in seif 3, because there the pronunciation itself does not change materially; the gentiles pronounce one expanded form and the Jews a shortened form. In our case, however, the final letter changes the preceding vowel and therefore the pronunciation itself differs. It therefore appears to me that we should write, "Arla, which is called Arle." I did not wish to rely on my own judgment alone and ask the master's view. There is also water here without a specific name. It appears unnecessary to name it, because it is only a pond and falls under ordinary springs as in Maharik. We should therefore write simply, "waters of wells and waters of springs," without naming a river. Please instruct us. The author's answer was: Study Responsa Maharik and the rulings of Terumat HaDeshen, from which the Rama's gloss here derives. You will see explicitly that the established Jewish-language name is primary. Rothenburg is written in Jewish usage with a final kaf and in gentile usage with a final gimel; the examples of Teivra and Tovra likewise involve different vocalization; and Kazmir, which is called Kazimiro in the Cracow get formula, differs by several letters. Certainly, where the difference is merely one vowel point we follow the Jewish-language form. This is what I found. No doubt my father and teacher had more to say, but the year brought calamity and his words were lost. May Hashem quench our thirst. I copied these few words as halachic guidance, not as a practical ruling.

en_segments: These are like three years. Knesset HaGedolah writes in the name of Maharshal that according to Rashbam the halacha follows Rav, who requires complete years. This is surprising, for where in Rashbam do we find that the halacha follows Rav and requires three complete years from day to day? Rashbam wrote only that according to this formulation even Shmuel does not reduce the period below three years, and this is how we rule. That language can be understood to mean that we rule like Shmuel. Moreover, even that language is not Rashbam's but Rabbeinu Chananel's. Rashbam may still hold that the halacha follows Shmuel, so that three harvests create a chazakah even in less than three years. Maharshal says that he found no one who rules like Rav except what he himself wrote in explanation of Rashbam, and he already rejected that reading. Yet I am astonished, because Rashbam writes explicitly, s.v. 'the words of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael,' that the Sages say their chazakah is three years from day to day, and that the opening sugya explains the reason for three years as, 'until three years a person is careful with his document, afterward he is no longer careful.' Rashbam then says that we rule like these Sages according to Rav, as is demonstrated by the sugya, which does not follow the gathering of three fruits from three years but requires three complete years in every case, because a person does not preserve his document for more than three years. Ramban likewise writes in his novellae that the statement, 'until three years a person is careful with his document,' compelled Rashbam to rule like Rav. See there.

en_segments: I later repurchased it. The Rambam omits Rav Yehudah's statement that if the claimant says, "I later repurchased it from him," he is believed. The Beit Yosef wonders why the Rambam omitted this law. The Lechem Mishneh answers that the rule was too obvious to require mention, because according to the Rif's interpretation the case is one where the orphans themselves held the field for three years and their predecessor held it for one day. In such a case it is self-evident that a claim of purchase is believed. But according to the Rif's reading, if the case already involves three years of possession, what does Rav Yehudah teach by saying that if he claims, "I bought it," he is believed? Did we not already know throughout the entire chapter Chazakat HaBatim that one who possesses land for three years and claims purchase is believed? The statement must teach something additional. The case must therefore be that Reuven came and challenged Shimon, saying that Shimon occupied a field stolen from him, and Reuven brought witnesses that Shimon had stolen it. Beit din removed Shimon and restored the field to Reuven. Reuven then possessed it for three years. Afterward Shimon produced the earlier document in which Reuven had signed as a witness identifying the boundary as Shimon's field, which amounts to an admission of Shimon's ownership. Reuven is nevertheless believed to say that after making that boundary identification he later purchased the field from Shimon. The Ran explains similarly. At first glance this is difficult. Reuven initially came with a claim of robbery. One who says, "you stole this field from me," necessarily says that he did not purchase it from the alleged robber. Once the signed boundary document establishes that Reuven had admitted Shimon's title, how can Reuven later change his story and say, "I then bought it from you"? Has he not already been established as contradicting himself by having claimed that the field was in Shimon's possession by robbery? Rav Yehudah therefore teaches a significant point. Reuven's earlier statement that the field was stolen concerned the field as a whole. He was not required to distinguish one narrow strip within it. That strip may indeed have belonged to Shimon at the time Reuven identified it as Shimon's boundary, and Reuven later purchased that strip from him. Reuven's later explanation is not considered retracting and asserting a new claim, because his original accusation of robbery addressed the field generally and did not necessarily deny Shimon's ownership of that particular strip. This is a substantial novelty and explains the Ran's statement that the challenger had earlier recovered the field, meaning necessarily on a robbery claim. Accordingly, the question regarding the Rambam returns. If Rav Yehudah's ruling is not obvious, why did the Rambam omit it? Tosafot on 30a likewise say that the claimant had possessed the property and that the novelty is that we might have thought he is not believed because he challenged the other person's ownership before the three years of chazakah, and people do not ordinarily purchase from someone whose ownership they have just disputed. This accords with what was explained. It appears that the Rambam understands the case differently. The challenger had already been in possession of the land from earlier times. Then the other person produced the boundary deed on which the challenger had signed as a witness, creating an admission that the strip belonged to the other. The challenger answers that after that admission he later repurchased the strip and then again possessed the field for three years. According to Rashbam's explanation on 39b regarding the requirement to renew a protest every three years, Rashbam rejects the view that the reason is lest the possessor later say, "after your protest I bought it from you." Rashbam holds that once the possessor initially entered without a lawful purchase, he is not later believed merely by continued possession to say that he subsequently acquired it. Applied here, the challenger's possession before he made the boundary identification was effectively an admission that his earlier entry as to the disputed strip had not been lawful. One might therefore think that he could no longer claim that the strip later came into his hands by purchase, because before the boundary deed he had occupied it without valid title. Rav Yehudah teaches that since the field as a whole had genuinely been his from earlier times, his continued possession after the admission can support the claim that he later repurchased this particular strip. This may explain why the Rambam regarded the ruling as subsumed within broader principles and did not state it separately. From this point onward, unfortunately, material is missing from the manuscript until siman 149, seif katan 8, and some sections of siman 150 are likewise missing. Many valuable discussions were contained there. It is a great loss.

en_segments: When does this apply? When he sold it in one document. See Sema, seif katan 19. Rif and Rambam make no distinction at all between one deed and several deeds, and Rosh and other poskim question them. In my view Rif and Rambam are primary, and their approach resolves numerous difficulties in Ketubot 99. The Gemara asks: if a principal told an agent, "Sell a kor," and he sold half a kor, do we say, "You improved matters for me," or does the principal say, "I do not want numerous documents against me"? The Gemara first attempts proof from the Mishnah in Me'ilah where an agent was given a gold dinar to buy a cloak and bought a cloak for only part of the money and another item with the rest. The Mishnah says the owner commits me'ilah. If partial performance were a deviation, why should the owner be liable? The Gemara answers that the agent obtained goods worth the full amount for a reduced price. It then brings the Mishnah concerning a widow whose ketubah was four hundred zuz and who sold separate parcels worth one hundred, with only the last sale containing overcharge, and says the earlier sales stand. The Gemara ultimately distinguishes small parcels and then records the dispute whether an instruction to sell to "one" means exactly one buyer or allows several. The difficulty is that the initial formulation itself seems contradictory. If the only issue were whether partial sale benefits the principal, then absent benefit it should be a deviation. Yet the alternative formulation suggests that only an actual disadvantage, namely many deeds, makes it a deviation, implying that absent disadvantage the agent would not be treated as deviating. Mishneh LaMelech explains a general dispute in several places: where an agent departs from the principal's wording but the departure is neither beneficial nor harmful, is the wording merely descriptive or strictly limiting? If the change is beneficial, everyone agrees there is no insistence. If the change is harmful, everyone agrees the principal is particular. Accordingly, the Gemara's question is posed according to both views. According to the strict-wording view, perhaps selling gradually is nevertheless a benefit and therefore allowed. According to the descriptive-language view, perhaps the burden of multiple deeds is an actual disadvantage and therefore the principal is particular. The Gemara first resolves the first branch from Me'ilah. There, proliferation of documents is irrelevant, yet partial purchase counts as performance. This proves that partial execution can be considered beneficial. It also fits the general halachah that wording is strict where no benefit exists. The Gemara then turns to the second branch and tests whether multiple deeds are itself a genuine disadvantage. It cites the widow's sales. Ritva explains that if multiple deeds were considered a real disadvantage, a widow who needs to sell everything on one day should not be allowed to divide the sale among multiple deeds. The Mishnah therefore shows that multiple deeds are not regarded as a legal disadvantage. When the Gemara then says "this too indicates," it concludes that the agent who sold only half a kor is nevertheless treated as deviating, because although multiple deeds are not a legal disadvantage, selling half is also not an actual benefit sufficient to override the principal's strict wording. Thus the principal's statement "a kor" is treated as limiting. This explains Rif and Rambam. They rule like Rav Chisda that an instruction "to one" can include several buyers, because multiple deeds are not considered a legal disadvantage. Yet they also rule that if one said "sell a kor" and the agent sold half, the agent deviated. There is no contradiction. The latter rule does not depend on the number of deeds. It depends on the principal's specific quantity instruction, which is controlling where the agent cannot show a genuine benefit. This also explains why they do not distinguish whether the first half was already transferred by a separate document or whether both halves might ultimately be included in one deed. Once "a kor" is treated as an exact instruction, the principal can retract from the partial transaction, just as in siman 200 one can retract even from the last se'ah where the unit price was stated for the entire kor. The halachah thus follows the strict-wording approach. Wherever the agent materially changes the principal's stated instruction, such as selling half when instructed to sell a whole kor, or selling to two when explicitly told "to one," the transaction is void unless the change is shown to be an actual benefit. But if the principal merely said "sell" without specifying one buyer, a sale to several buyers stands, because there is no departure from the instruction and the multiplication of deeds is not itself treated as harm. This also resolves the question from Even HaEzer, siman 103, concerning the widow. A widow selling to satisfy her ketubah is not an ordinary agent subject to the principal's exact language. Therefore, once multiple deeds are shown not to be harmful, her prior sales stand even without limiting the Mishnah to unusually small parcels. The "small parcels" answer was necessary only under the intermediate assumption that multiple deeds might itself be harmful. Accordingly, in my view the halachah follows Rif and Rambam rather than Mechaber's distinction between one deed and several. The decisive factor is not the number of documents, but whether the agent changed an express instruction of the principal. When the principal said "a kor" and the agent sold half, or said "to one" and the agent sold to several, the sale is void because of the change. When the principal spoke without such limitation, the sale stands.

en_segments: (Shach, seif katan 6) And this resolves the Bach's question against Rambam. Note: This requires examination. Perhaps where the borrower claims that his pledge was worth three dinarim, while according to the lender it was worth only a shekel, the borrower can say: "According to your own words I have a certain claim against you that the garment burned before witnesses was not mine. My garment was worth three dinarim, while you say the garment that burned was worth only a shekel." The Ramah's case, however, is where the depositor himself is uncertain, as explained in the Tur. A further difficulty with the Ramah is that otherwise every guardian who sets his eyes on a deposit could fraudulently arrange for a similar object to be lost before witnesses. He would not care about the loss of that substitute object, because he would keep the deposited object he desires. It is therefore advantageous to him to sacrifice the lesser object. The Ramah's words indicate that he stated his rule only where it is certainly known that the object was lost through an unavoidable accident and not through negligence caused by the guardian. In such a case there is no basis for suspicion. This can answer the Bach's question: Rava's answer that there are witnesses that the garment burned must, according to authorities who hold a lender on a pledge is not liable for unavoidable accidents, concern negligence. Since there was negligence, one can suspect that because the lender desired the pledge he caused the burning of his own low-value garment so that he could retain the valuable pledge. Rambam writes in the chapter Shevuat HaDayanim, in the mishnah concerning one who lends on a pledge, that even if the lender says to the owner, "I value it more than you claim it was worth," we still consider the possibility that he set his eyes upon it.

en_segments: tzadi) Ibid., seif 12, from Rami bar Chama's unresolved questions there. The Maggid Mishneh writes in law 9 that Rashi explains the first four questions where the owner was not present. His wording is: 'If he borrowed it for intercourse with it himself, is he liable for unavoidable accidents?' The issue is whether the borrowing for which the Torah imposed liability for unavoidable accidents is specifically ordinary borrowing, and similarly for the other cases. According to this explanation, if he borrowed it while the owner was present he is certainly exempt. In my humble opinion, Rashi's words imply that he remains liable for theft and loss like a paid guardian, as the Tur writes in the name of the Ramah, that if there is a benefit worth a perutah he is liable as a paid guardian. The explanatory phrase means that he wishes to appear wealthy and important, so that householders will not refrain from extending him credit, Rashi.

he_segments: [ש"ך בא"ד] דאינו אלא מדרבנן. נ"ב ורע"ק דאף אחרי נמכר גאולה תהי' לו הוי אסמכתא כ"כ היש"ש שם ותמוה לי הא אמרי' בבכורות דף יג הניח' למ"ד גזל נכרי אסור וכו' וכן בפ' המקבל גבי כרם רעיך הניח' למ"ד גזל נכרי הרי מדמצרכי' קרא באונאה ובכרם מוכח דמ"ד גזל נכרי אסור היינו מדאו' וצע"ג:

גם ראיתי בדפוס ש"ס הישנים (כי בדפוס החדשים השמיטו) דאית' שם בב"ק ישראל ונכרי שבאו לדון באי' עליו בעקיפין דברי ר"י רע"ק אומר אין באי' מפני קידוש השם טעמא דאיכא קידוש השם הא ליכא ק"ה באי' וכו' כאן בגזילה כאן בהפקעת הלואה הרי מפורש דלרע"ק דאוריית' אסור:
en_segments: [Shach, continuation of his words] That it is only rabbinically prohibited. Note: Regarding Rabbi Akiva, that even after he has been sold, the verse, “he shall have redemption,” is merely an asmachta, so writes the Yam Shel Shlomo there. This is astonishing to me, for in Bechorot 13a the Gemara says: This is satisfactory according to the one who holds that robbing a non-Jew is prohibited, etc. Likewise, in Perek HaMekabel, regarding “your fellow’s vineyard,” it says: This is satisfactory according to the one who holds that robbing a non-Jew is prohibited. Since Scripture is required regarding overreaching and regarding a vineyard, it is evident that according to the view that robbing a non-Jew is prohibited, the prohibition is by Torah law. This requires great study. I also saw in the old printings of the Talmud, for it was omitted in the newer printings, that in Bava Kamma it states: If a Jew and a non-Jew came for judgment, one may circumvent him, according to Rabbi Yishmael; Rabbi Akiva says that one may not circumvent him because of sanctification of Hashem’s Name. The implication is that only where there is sanctification of Hashem’s Name is it prohibited, but where there is no sanctification of Hashem’s Name it is permitted, etc. The Gemara distinguishes: here it concerns robbery, and there it concerns evasion of a debt. Thus it is explicit that according to Rabbi Akiva, robbery is prohibited by Torah law.
